topic.title: You're paying for the box
topic.claim: A heavy box makes a ₹500 product feel like ₹2,000, and brands now spend more on the unboxing than on the thing inside.
topic.moment: The magnetic flap, the tissue paper and the card that says 'you deserve this'.

turn.believed: Premium packaging means a premium product.
turn.actually: The box is built for the first thirty seconds, because that's the part that gets filmed and shared.

topic.because: Your unboxing reel is free ads for the brand. The product only has to be fine after that.
topic.payoff: Throw away the box in your head. Would you still pay this for what's left in your hand?
topic.behaviour: D2C brands invest in rigid boxes, inserts and notes; buyers film unboxings and post them.
topic.mechanism: Packaging buys free reach and a feeling of value, which is cheaper than improving the product.
topic.group: Online shoppers who buy D2C brands
topic.send_to: The friend who keeps every nice box 'just in case'.
topic.why_now: Gifting season means the box matters more than ever this month.

score.why: Premium packaging is built for the first thirty seconds that get filmed; the box is the ad.

cover.headline: That heavy box was built for your [camera], not your cream
cover.sub: Brands spend on the moment you film, then the jar just has to be fine.

paragraphs: That heavy box was built for your camera, not your cream.
slides.why_swipe: Which box, and what's wrong with filming it?

paragraphs: The parcel finally comes on a lazy Saturday. You slit the tape with your house keys, and the magnetic flap lets go with a soft *thup*.
Tissue paper, a sticker seal, a little card that says "you deserve this". Your phone is out before the jar is.
slides.why_swipe: What happens once the phone is out?

paragraphs: The first take looks dull, so you press the flap shut and open it again by the window. Story posted, brand tagged.
It feels like proof. A brand this careful with the outside must be just as careful with the inside.
slides.why_swipe: So was the inside as good as the box?

paragraphs: Three weeks in, the cream does exactly what your old chemist one did. Same smell, same feel on your face by evening.
The box is on top of your cupboard now, holding a charger and two rubber bands.
**The box was built for the first thirty seconds. The cream only had to be fine after that.**
slides.why_swipe: Why would a brand put the money into the box?

paragraphs: Because those thirty seconds were the ad. You shot it twice, tagged the brand and showed it to friends who trust you more than any banner.
The brand paid for one nice box. You paid the extra on the price, then made their ad for free.
And the *thup* felt good on a bad week. You just paid for that feeling twice: once in money, once in content.
slides.why_swipe: So where did that extra money actually end up?

paragraphs: The jar ran out last week.
**The part you paid extra for is still on top of your cupboard, holding a charger.**

end.save: Come back to it before you hit 'Place order' on this year's gifts.
end.send: The friend who keeps every nice box 'just in case'.
end.promise: How brands really sell to you.

draft.caption: The nicest thing I bought this year came with a magnetic flap, and it now holds my spare cables.
draft.alt_text: Carousel post. Cover headline: 'That heavy box was built for your camera, not your cream', with a sub-line saying brands spend on the moment you film, then the jar just has to be fine. The slides follow the reader opening a premium parcel with a magnetic flap, tissue paper and a 'you deserve this' card. They re-film the lid by the window because the first take looked dull, then post it and tag the brand. Weeks later the cream works just like their old chemist one, and the box sits on the cupboard holding a charger and rubber bands. The post argues the box is built for the filmed first thirty seconds, because the reader's story is free advertising, and that the reader paid for the feeling twice, in money and in content. It ends with the jar empty while the box, the part they paid extra for, still holds a charger.
